declared_absences.work: The Apocryphon of John (the Secret Book of John)
declared_absences.why: The foundational Sethian text, surviving in four manuscripts, and the closest thing Gnosticism has to a canonical scripture. No openly licensed machine-readable Coptic edition exists. Searched 2026-08-21: Coptic SCRIPTORIUM does not hold it; authenticated GitHub search returns one edition whose Coptic derives from scanned PDFs of Meyer 2007 and Linssen, relicensed CC BY-SA by a party that does not hold those rights; Schmidt 1905 is public domain but is the Pistis Sophia volume, and archive.org OCR strips Coptic script entirely; Till 1955, the Berlin Codex edition, remains in copyright.
declared_absences.ruling: Not seated rather than seated defectively. A corpus whose licence is asserted by a party who cannot grant it would place a rights defect inside the sovereign record — the failure this archive exists to document. Absent-and-declared over present-and-defective.
declared_absences.opening: One text, four witnesses. A synoptic open edition of the Apocryphon of John is the narrowest and highest-value gap in the openly licensed Coptic record.

corpora.why_seated: Plotinus is the strongest single comparandum for the Plato–Aristotle authorship question. Seven centuries and a dialect separate them. The seat exists so that result can be re-run and contested rather than reported.

corpora.why_seated: Asked for as the Book of Mormon, and seated only beside the other traditions that divided in the same years: in 1844 Joseph Smith was killed at Carthage (27 June) and the church he founded split over who should lead it, in the same months that the Bab declared his mission in Shiraz (22–23 May) and the Millerites waited for 22 October.
corpora.scope: The scripture as first printed and as revised: the Book of Mormon in the first edition (Palmyra, 1830) and the third, 'carefully revised by the translator' (Nauvoo, 1840); the revelations in the Book of Commandments (Zion, 1833), left unfinished when a mob destroyed the press, and in the Doctrine and Covenants of 1835 (Kirtland, with the Lectures on Faith) and 1845 (Nauvoo, the edition that announces the martyrdom). Then the succession itself: the Times and Seasons of September 1844, with the epistle of the Twelve and the trial of Sidney Rigdon, and James J. Strang's counter-claim from Voree, the Voree Herald of 1846 and The Diamond of 1848, with the letter of 18 June 1844 on which it rests. The 1837 Kirtland edition of the Book of Mormon was not found in an open scan: QUEUED. Strang's Book of the Law of the Lord (1851; 1856), the RLDS editions (from 1874; the Authorized Version of 1908) and the Pearl of Great Price (1851): QUEUED. Manuscripts held by the Joseph Smith Papers are under that project's terms and are not seated.

corpora.why_seated: The second tradition of 1844: the Bab declared his mission in Shiraz on 22–23 May 1844, five weeks before Joseph Smith was killed; after the Bab's execution (1850) his followers divided between Subh-i Azal and Baha'u'llah, as the Latter Day Saints divided between the Twelve and Strang.
corpora.scope: Both sides of the tradition that began in Shiraz on the night of 22–23 May 1844, when the Bab declared his mission to Mulla Husayn and began the Qayyum al-Asma'. The Bab: the Qayyum al-Asma' (Ahsan al-qisas) in the copy given by Mulla Husayn, the Persian Bayan, and Panj Sha'n, in the Iran National Baha'i Archives manuscripts. The division after him: Baha'u'llah's Kitab-i Iqan in the first lithograph (Bombay, c. 1882) and the Mishkin Qalam lithograph (Bombay, 1893), al-Kitab al-Aqdas in Tumanskii's St. Petersburg edition (1899), and 'Abdu'l-Baha's Traveller's Narrative in Browne's facsimile of the Persian (1891), on the Baha'i side; and the Kitab-i Nuqtatu'l-Kaf in Browne's edition (1910), the history Browne attributed to Hajji Mirza Jani and read as the Azali account, an attribution Baha'i scholarship disputes. Not seated: the UCLA manuscript of the Persian Bayan (a 199 MB scan, over the repository's file limit): QUEUED; the Arabic Bayan, found only in a 1962 printing; writings of Subh-i Azal in his own name, not found in an open edition in this pass: QUEUED; the Kitab-i Aqdas in the Tehran printing of c. 1943 that H-Bahai reproduces beside Tumanskii's; translations.

White's first visions in her Sketch of the Christian Experience and Views (Saratoga Springs, 1851). A Word to the 'Little Flock' (1847) was found only in a facsimile with a later foreword and is not seated. corpora.why_seated: The fourth tradition of 1844: in that year Hong Xiuquan and Feng Yunshan went out preaching into Guangxi, where the God Worshippers' Society took shape and from which the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom rose in 1851. Its scripture is a Bible rewritten and annotated by its king, beside the words of a God who spoke through Yang Xiuqing until Yang was killed in the Tianjing incident of 1856.
corpora.scope: The texts of the Taiping movement as Wikisource holds them: Hong Xiuquan's three Yuandao tracts, written in the years after his vision and before the rising (c. 1845–48); the books issued under the Heavenly King's seal (旨准頒行詔書), of which the movement's own list names twenty-nine, seated here as Wikisource has them: the Heavenly Father's edict, the two parts of the Heavenly Father's descent, the Book of Heavenly Decrees (1852), the Old and New Testaments as Hong revised and annotated them (1853), the Heavenly Commandments (1853), the proclamations, the Three Character Classic, the Ode for Youth (1852), the regulations, the ceremonial (1858), the Land System (1853), the Principles of the Heavenly Nature and the Essentials of Heavenly Principle (1854); Yang Xiuqing's Taiping Song of World Salvation; the Taiping Heavenly Chronicle (proclaimed 1848, printed 1862); and Hong Rengan's New Treatise (1859). Not seated: the books of the list Wikisource does not hold, among them the Taiping Imperial Declaration (太平詔書), the army organization (太平軍目) and the calendar (頒行曆書), and the Gospel of John of the Taiping New Testament: QUEUED, as are scans of the original Nanjing imprints (British Library and others) and the Taiping documents in Western collections. Translations (Medhurst, 1853; Michael, 1966–71) are not seated.
